scenes.text: So, when does complementary healthcare help? Name three things you, or someone you know, use for health that no doctor prescribed. For each one, what's it supposed to do, and how would you find out if it does? Now, which of the three would you tell a doctor about? And why not the others?

First, stop treating it as one thing. Complementary healthcare means products and services used alongside normal medical care. If they're used instead of it, that's alternative care, and the risks are completely different. Sort the category into five groups. Things you swallow: vitamins, herbal products, sports supplements. Practitioner services, like naturopathy, massage, acupuncture and chiropractic. Mind-body practices, like yoga, tai chi and meditation. Health apps and websites. And gadgets sold with health claims. The evidence base, how much research backs each one, runs from good to almost none. And in Australia, a listed product has had its ingredients drawn from a low-risk list, but nobody has checked that it works.

Prevention is where it's used most, and where the case is strongest, because prevention is about habits you keep up. The evidence is reasonable for mind-body practices easing stress and long-term pain, and for tai chi and yoga improving balance and strength, which helps prevent falls in older people. Supplements are weaker. They correct a shortfall, but they don't add benefit once you have enough. And often the real ingredient is time. A practitioner who listens for an hour and follows up is giving attention, continuity and support to change, which genuinely work, and which a short appointment struggles to give. Two risks. Money spent on things that don't work isn't spent on things that do. And a product can push out something proven, like an immunity supplement taken instead of a vaccine.

Using it to treat a health issue gives the best evidence for some things and the biggest harm for others. What decides it isn't the therapy. It's whether it's used instead of effective treatment, or alongside it. The claims that hold up are narrow, like some manual therapies for some back pain, or mindfulness for chronic pain. Broad claims, to detox, boost immunity or cure serious disease, aren't supported. A treatment that works for everything works for nothing in particular. And the serious harm is rarely the therapy itself. It's the delay. Choosing an alternative for a serious, treatable illness uses up the window when treatment works. Cancer is the best-studied case, and delayed treatment there means worse survival.

Most often, it's used alongside medical treatment. Think of someone having chemotherapy who uses acupuncture for nausea, or someone with back pain using medicine, physio and yoga together. It can help, because medical treatment often targets the disease, while anxiety, pain and sleep get less attention, and feeling in control helps people stick with treatment. The real issue is telling. Many people don't tell their doctor, often because nobody asks, or they expect to be dismissed. That matters, because of interactions, where one substance changes how another works. Some herbal products strengthen blood thinners, change how the liver handles drugs, or raise bleeding risk in surgery. The danger isn't the product. It's the secret.

And it loops. Dismissal leads to silence, silence leaves the risk unseen, and that feeds more dismissal. The doctor has to break it, by asking every patient, without judgement, and putting everything on one plan.

So put it on a grid with two questions. Is it used alongside medical care, or instead of it? And has the person told the people treating them? Alongside and told is the safest. Alongside but not told is the common risk, interactions. Instead of, but told, at least means someone knows what's being given up. Instead of and not told is the most dangerous, because nobody knows to step in. All of this assumes the problem needs treatment. For a mild one that clears up on its own, instead of matters much less. To explain this well, judge specific uses, not the whole category. Take people's reasons seriously: rushed care, wanting control, culture and belief. Be precise about the risks: delay, interactions and cost. And notice what popularity says about the system: people want time and attention, and they'll pay for it.
Two things to remember. Alongside or instead? That decides the risk. And the danger is the secret.

Two exam questions. First. Person one declines recommended treatment for an early, curable cancer, choosing a diet plan instead, and has told their doctor. Person two drinks a herbal tea for mild seasonal symptoms instead of an over-the-counter medicine, and hasn't told anyone. For each, name the grid cell, the main risk, and your advice. Pause here to answer.

Person one is instead of, but told. The risk is losing the window when the cancer is curable, so the advice is to keep the effective treatment, and use the diet alongside it if they want. Person two is instead of and not told, but for a mild problem that clears up on its own, so the risk is low. Review it if it persists. The classic mistake is judging the product, not how it's used.

Second. A man with high blood pressure stops his prescribed tablets after a naturopath recommends a herbal preparation and a diet plan. He hasn't told his GP. Explain the risks, and one way the health system could reduce them. Pause here to answer.

This is instead of, and not told, the most dangerous cell. Stopping proven treatment leaves his blood pressure uncontrolled, raising the risk of stroke and heart attack, and nobody knows to step in. The herb may also interact with anything else he takes. The fix is in the system: GPs asking every patient about complementary use, without judgement, so it goes on one plan. The classic mistake is blaming the man.

So sort the category, ask alongside or instead, ask who's been told, and judge the use, not the label. Now take one product off the shelf. Read its label. Clinically proven to boost immunity. Doctors recommend. How do you decide whether to believe it?
